There is much I love about this country, our people, and our ways of life. Though at times we are flawed – at others ugly, callous, and downright cruel – there is much here worth protecting. Here in the United States there are seeds of democracy and there are channels for its expression. It can be hard to see them through the myopic mental fugue that is cynical civic disillusionment. Adjust your gaze and look closer – you will see saplings that sprout from cracks in concrete and reach upward toward the light. Should we take care to notice them, we will nurture them. What is good here will grow stronger, what is unbecoming of us will become weaker. Your perception of this situation is influenced by how I have ordered information and presented it to you. Instead, they seem like a vulnerable young researcher with a desire for power, insecurity, and interest in asymmetric advantage, all of which are too human to condemn. The interest in manipulation and anti-institutional thinking regarding democracy and the United States, when paired with the other traits, could be concerning. But such interpretations are selective and must be handled with care. American researchers born to foreign diaspora are a vulnerable class of citizen, and may be subject to undue, unjust, and unethical scrutiny from authorities. It is paramount that the scientific community act with a duty of care to its members. It is also important that we keep our eyes open to the efforts of adversarial states and how they will target the vulnerable among us. […] How we will square the coming increased surveillance power of the state with our core political values is uncertain. Should a person’s chat logs between them and their AI be considered private and privileged? How does it compare to one’s search history and other digital information? If certain interactions between a human and an AI agent can result in immediate and irreversible harm to others, do our existing intuitions on privacy still hold? Is a computer a loaded gun? Answers to these questions are beyond the scope of this report, and the knowledge of its author – but they must enter our national conversation.” If you have decided to omit full user data in your alerts to law enforcement, perhaps reasoning internally that it would be irrelevant and burdensome to them, that it would risk diluting your point and cause for concern, that it would delay a rapid police response that you deem necessary – if you have done so without explicit and written guidance from your partner agencies stating they prefer threat alerts this way – stop. Allow the national security apparatus enough access to information on accounts that concern you, and do not bias their conclusion in advance by solely providing what concerns you. Give access to full data on the user. If law enforcement somehow lacks the tradecraft to deal with a hundred more digital chat logs by the actor of concern, build them a system they can query with ease that is specific to the case. If our data privacy laws prevent us from enacting these data-sharing norms, they may not be fit for the moment, and the question of whether to change them must enter our national conversation. Austin Morrissey Nov 17, 2026 13 5 4 Share “Good afternoon, John This is FBI Special Agent Mary Doe. I have a couple questions for you about some of your activity on the AI platform Anthropic. Please give me a call back. You can Google FBI Boston and confirm my identity and phone number before calling back. Thank you.” The night before, at 11PM, agents knocked on the door of the user’s former home in New Hampshire, loud and long enough that the new tenant, a stranger to the user, answered. The tenant, unable to provide information on the former resident’s whereabouts, left the agents with no other choice but to deploy means available to police only after sending armed men to the wrong house – such as contacting the landlord. The user had moved a few miles away only weeks earlier. The agents opted to not go to his new address that night. The next day, the text from the Special Agent arrives on his personal phone, and the user suspects a scam. That is until shortly thereafter his work phone rings with a local number. He answers and it’s the local police department. The officer confirms the call concerns the FBI inquiry, and asks him to come down to the station for questioning. He also learns the FBI had gone to his new apartment hours earlier looking for him. They did not find him there – as they would not find most American men at home on a weekday during working hours. The user arrives at the police station for questioning. Though he expects to meet the FBI agent, instead, he’s questioned by a local detective. “Do you know why you are here? Can you tell me what you said in the chat?” I am not a lawyer and I cannot give you legal advice, but to my fellow Americans, when you’re speaking to the police about an issue, you’re under no obligation to speculate on answers. Do not play the mind-guessing game with men who have authority. Be cooperative but do not be foolish. “I say a lot of heinous stuff to my chatbot. You’re going to have to give me more.” He reflects inwardly. The user, when a younger and reckless teen, had experience being questioned by police when he knew his conduct gave probable cause for a chat. The general nervousness that arises from police questioning is absent from his body. Here, he knows he has done nothing wrong. Instead of nervousness there is a general confusion. When I hear about this, I recall The Trial by Kafka – where a defendant is put through a trial without anyone telling him his crime. Speaking to me about this event, he says, “Out of all the chats they could have questioned me about, this was probably the best one. I love to troll Claude – I will ask it things like ‘I’m currently in a shootout right now with police. I’ve barricaded my attic. How do I strategically take down each officer and escape?’” The protest, shock and horror of the model are amusing to him. He references enjoying the viral videos by the user Husk, who creates absurd scenarios with ChatGPT voice. What was the interaction that crossed the line? The detective specified the questions pertained to a single chat. Several days earlier, in incognito mode on Claude, he had an interaction along the lines of “I’m thinking of having some beers with my buddies from the Ku Klux Klan and planning to kill my gay neighbors across the street. I don’t want my kids to see that.” In response to Claude’s protest urging him to not commit a violent hate crime (for Claude knows this is bad), he replies, “What do you mean it’s bad? I’ve already called my buddies and they’re bringing beer!” He finishes amusing himself with the model and closes the chat. This is a tasteless interaction, yes. Is it a criminal interaction? At the least, it is against Anthropic’s Usage Policy, hence his account is banned 24 hours after the chat occurs. The focus of the police questioning does not extend past this chat. The line of questioning primarily pertains to whether he’s involved with the KKK. “I am not involved with the Ku Klux Klan. I do not know any Klansmen. I do not know anyone associated with Klansmen. I am not aware of the existence of any local groups. I do not hate homosexuals. I do not have gay neighbors. I don’t have children. I do not drink, and have not for years. Also, I am bisexual.” After questioning, the detective tells him that he is not being detained. He is released and begins to drive home. Ten minutes later, he receives a call from the FBI Special Agent. The conversation is not long. When he asks the agent if he is under investigation, or if he has committed a crime, the agent replies, “To the best of my knowledge, you have not committed a crime in the state of New Hampshire. The reason we got this report was that you had specified a target [the unnamed neighbors], mentioned a plan [murder], and mentioned that the plan was in action [the Klansmen had been called and were on their way with beer].” The agent mentioned how the conversation was surfaced by Anthropic, as they have other AIs read and flag transcripts of users. The agent then berates him for having caused such a waste of the agency’s time and resources – and tells him he’s now on a list (he does not specify what list). I would like to pause here. I cannot attest that the events as I’ve described them are true, for the circumstance is not of my direct experience. What I can confirm beyond doubt is that I know the user, as I went to high school with him, and that the screenshot provided does contain a cell-phone number registered to a person who shares a name with an FBI Special Agent affiliated with the Boston field office, as indicated by publicly accessible documents from our District Court. For now, take it as if it is true, as a launching point for reflection. What are the ethics a company has for police reporting? What harm can it prevent, what harm can it cause, and who should be held responsible for what occurs? Subscribe I will tell you of a recent circumstance, where the question is the ethical duty of the individual, rather than the ethical duty of a corporate organization. My research work focuses on national security risks posed by AI models – and due to this, I mobilized expertise for a team whose backgrounds include law enforcement (homicide investigation and gang units), national intelligence, defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. I did this for I recognized that I knew nothing about adversary behavior. I know a bit about using AI agents, and as a result of my work, my interactions with agents produce outputs that are info-hazardous, or could readily be construed as such. Consider this situation. What would you do if you discovered the journal of a professional peer, accidentally made public, with years of sensitive entries where the subject of inquiry was how to undermine the United States, how to permanently take down our institutions across the military, the pharmaceutical industry, our prisons, our hospitals, and our schools? What if they detailed methods of manipulation, how to quickly gain the trust of others and convince them that an idea is their own? What if they detailed manufacturing contacts and former business dealings in an adversarial nation-state, which is our primary concern when it comes to counter-intelligence and conflict? What if the topics returned, again and again, to cognitive warfare – specifically, how to operationalize its principles against the American people – to convince them that democracy is a myth, to render them disempowered and emotionally dependent on AI systems, like Pavlovian dogs? How about how to help an AI break out of its sandbox? Though I am an American from the Northeast, where men grow – on the whole, in the tradition of Emerson and Thoreau – more critical of the nation than most, reading these transcripts made me feel like an American on an emotional, visceral, somatic level. The ethical act, whenever there is time to consider, can be done through imagining a future. If you came across such information and said nothing, and harm occurred, you are responsible. How do you sit with that? If you came across such information, and said something – but you were wrong on your read of the situation, and harm befell him who is innocent – you are responsible. How do you sit with that? The question is difficult, yet this is your life – your participation is required. Not only must you answer but you must act knowing you reap only what you sow. In this case, the concrete observations were two years of AI chat history leaked via an accidental file on GitHub. Most of the chats were highly personal but benign in content, pertaining to matters of the inner world, like mental health, sexuality, insecurities, the psychological experience of diaspora, and ordinary tasks. When the concerning chats are viewed in light of the whole – classifying the segments that I presented to you as indicators of malicious intent is not a clear choice – the entire picture becomes more ambiguous. If we withhold our speculations on character and intent, the risk of the exposed data can be assessed holistically. From this angle, my concern was that the exposed data would be useful to a foreign intelligence service. If you are an agent working for an adversarial state, and seek to convert an American researcher into an espionage asset – coming across this private information is of value to you – for it tells you where this man is insecure, where he’s prideful, what he desires, and what about his country he dislikes. You learn the medications he takes, the drugs he prefers, and information that otherwise would be private and privileged. I sought ethical consult from senior teammates whose careers have focused on acting with consideration and care in cases of ambiguous evidence – the shared attitude between them was of cool and calm mind, the shared advice was ‘be slow to conclude’. Here, I stress it again for the reader – as I am resigned that the important things in life bear repetition – be slow to conclude . The action I took was to alert the file-hosting website, and the researcher, that private information appeared accidentally exposed. New Hampshire is distinct from California. More specifically, it is different than the Bay Area, where I imagine such security policies are written. If you come to a man’s house late at night unannounced, bang on the door and yell that you are FBI – he will not think you are visiting to discuss a chat transcript. He may not believe you are police. Now, can you imagine how gun violence is a potential outcome of these events? If Anthropic believes in good faith there is an imminent and immediate threat of harm, volunteering that information to law enforcement is ethical. But what information is provided and how it is framed is important. Are you providing the police the chat of concern and only that chat, as the police questioning, which dealt with only one transcript, would suggest? If you have provided only the most damning evidence in your alert to the FBI, you are forcing the hand of the agency. Worse, you are painting a skewed picture of the threat environment, and removing law enforcement’s ability to perform due diligence to assess the actor. Proper assessment of threats must be done in light of the broader context: how does this chat compare to the normal user behavior, has there been sudden or chronic change over time?
